prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My first week in Cambridge a car full of white boys tried to run me off the road, and spit through the window, open to ask directions. I was always asking directions and always driving: to an Armenian market in Watertown to buy figs and string cheese, apricots, dark spices and olives from barrels, tubes of paste with unreadable Arabic labels. I ate stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the mirror. The floors of my apartment would never come clean. Whenever I saw other colored people in bookshops, or museums, or cafeterias, I’d gasp, smile shyly, but they’d disappear before I spoke. What would I have said to them? Come with me? Take me home? Are you my mother? No. I sat alone in countless Chinese restaurants eating almond cookies, sipping tea with spoons and spoons of sugar. Popcorn and coffee was dinner. When I fainted from migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man above me mouthed: “No breakfast.” He gave me orange juice and chocolate bars. The color red sprang into relief singing Wagner’s Walküre. Entire tribes gyrated and drummed in my head. I learned the samba from a Brazilian man so tiny, so festooned with glitter I was certain that he slept inside a filigreed, Fabergé egg. No one at the door: no salesmen, Mormons, meter readers, exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, no one. Red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.

Keywords: Cambridge, Armenian, Watertown

During my first week in Cambridge, a car full of white boys tried to run me off the road and spat through the window I had opened to ask for directions. I was always asking directions and always driving: to an Armenian market in Watertown to buy figs and string cheese, apricots, dark spices, olives from barrels, and tubes of paste with unreadable Arabic labels. When I fainted from a migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man standing above me mouthed, “No breakfast.” He gave me orange juice and chocolate bars.

outputs.L2:
During my first week in Cambridge, a group of white boys packed into a car attempted to force me off the road and spat through the window I had lowered to request directions. I was forever getting lost and forever behind the wheel, traveling to an Armenian grocery in Watertown for figs, string cheese, apricots, deep-colored spices, barrel-packed olives, and tubes of paste marked with Arabic writing I could not decipher. I ate grape leaves filled with stuffing, then studied my swelling lips in the mirror.

No amount of scrubbing could make the floors in my apartment clean. In bookstores, museums, and cafeterias, the sight of another person of color made me catch my breath and offer a timid smile, but each one vanished before I could speak. And what could I have asked? Come along with me? Bring me home? Are you my mother? Of course not.

I spent innumerable meals by myself in Chinese restaurants, nibbling almond cookies and loading my tea with spoonful after spoonful of sugar. Some nights, dinner consisted only of popcorn and coffee. Once, a migraine caused me to collapse in a grocery store. A Portuguese man leaned over me and silently formed the words, “No breakfast.” Then he brought me orange juice and chocolate bars.

Red suddenly became vivid while I sang Wagner’s *Walküre*. Whole tribes danced and beat drums inside my skull. A diminutive Brazilian man taught me the samba; he was covered in so much glitter that I felt sure he slept within an ornate Fabergé egg of filigree. Nobody ever appeared at my door—not salespeople, Mormons, utility-meter inspectors, pest-control workers, Harriet Tubman, or anyone else. Crimson notes rang through a drab town of trolley cars.
outputs.L3:
During her first week in Cambridge, the narrator quickly discovers how hostile and alienating the city can be. While she is driving, a group of white boys attempts to force her car off the road and spits at her. The incident is not only frightening but also a brutal reminder that, as a woman of color, she is vulnerable to racist harassment even in ordinary public spaces. This early encounter shapes her perception of Cambridge as a gray, unwelcoming place where she does not feel safe or accepted.

In response, she searches for comfort through movement, familiar sights, and sensory experiences. Driving gives her a temporary sense of freedom and control, while visits to ethnic markets allow her to encounter foods, languages, and customs associated with different cultures. She eats meals from a variety of traditions, using taste and smell to create moments of warmth in an unfamiliar environment. These experiences help her resist the city’s bleakness and reconnect, however briefly, with a broader multicultural world.

Despite this search for familiarity, the narrator remains profoundly isolated. She longs to speak with other people of color, imagining that they might understand her feelings of displacement, yet she cannot bring herself to approach them. Their presence offers the possibility of connection, but her uncertainty and emotional exhaustion keep her at a distance. As a result, she continues to move through the city alone, observing potential communities without feeling able to join them.

Her loneliness gradually affects her physical well-being. She neglects basic self-care, eats by herself, and struggles to maintain a healthy routine. Eventually, a severe migraine causes her to collapse. At this vulnerable moment, a Portuguese man comes to her aid, bringing her food and juice. His simple act of kindness contrasts sharply with the hostility she encountered earlier and provides a rare experience of human care and solidarity.

Throughout the narrative, music, dance, food, and vivid multicultural encounters create flashes of color and vitality within Cambridge’s otherwise oppressive grayness. These moments do not erase the narrator’s fear or loneliness, but they offer brief relief and suggest the possibility of belonging. In a city that often feels cold and exclusionary, cultural expression and unexpected kindness become sources of comfort, reminding her that warmth and connection can still emerge in unlikely places.
outputs.L4:
My first week in Cambridge survives in my memory not as a continuous story but as a series of sharp, disconnected impressions: wet stone beneath a colorless sky, the sour smell of my damp coat, bicycle bells ringing behind me, and faces that seemed to close whenever I approached. The cold entered through my shoes and settled in my bones. I was always walking—between unfamiliar buildings, along streets whose names I could not yet pronounce, through courtyards that looked ancient and self-assured. Everything around me appeared to belong exactly where it was. I alone seemed misplaced.

Some people stared at me openly. Others spoke slowly and loudly, as if my accent were a sign that I could not understand English. A shopkeeper watched my hands instead of my face. In a crowded room, a student asked where I was “really” from and then praised my English before I could answer. These incidents were small enough to be dismissed by anyone who did not experience them, yet they accumulated until I felt that my presence required explanation. I became intensely conscious of my skin, my voice, my clothes, and every movement I made.

Loneliness followed me even in crowds. I missed the ease of familiar gestures and the comfort of being surrounded by people who understood the references hidden inside my speech. In Cambridge, conversation seemed governed by rules everyone else had learned long ago. Jokes passed too quickly. Names of schools, towns, books, and traditions carried meanings I could not grasp. By the time I understood what was being discussed, the subject had changed.

The physical difficulties made everything worse. My room was colder than I had expected, and the radiator offered more noise than heat. I woke early, stiff and exhausted, and dressed beneath the blankets. Rain appeared without warning and left my hair, notebooks, and sleeves damp for hours. I had too little money, too little food, and no idea where to buy the things I needed. Even ordinary tasks—finding a bus, ordering a meal, asking for directions—became tests of endurance.

Yet the week was not without moments of grace. A stranger held a door when my arms were full. Someone in a café smiled without curiosity or condescension and showed me where to leave my tray. One evening, another international student invited me to share a meal. The table was crowded with dishes from several countries: rice fragrant with spices, bread still warm from the oven, bright sauces, pickled vegetables, and sweets wrapped in paper. We exchanged names, mispronounced them, corrected one another, and laughed.

Music offered another kind of refuge. From a room at the end of a corridor came a song whose rhythm I recognized before I recognized the language. I stood outside listening until the door opened and someone pulled me inside. Soon chairs had been pushed back and people were dancing—awkwardly at first, then with abandon. For a few minutes, the grayness of the city gave way to color. Bodies moved without explanation. Accents ceased to matter. I did not have to describe where I came from or defend my right to be there.

Those moments did not erase the racism, homesickness, or exhaustion. Their very briefness made my isolation more visible. After the meal, I still returned to a cold room; after the dancing, the corridor was silent again. But each act of kindness became something I could carry with me. Each shared taste, melody, and movement suggested that belonging might not be granted all at once. Perhaps it could be assembled slowly, from fragments: a warm plate passed across a table, a familiar rhythm heard through a wall, a hand extended before I had learned how to ask.
outputs.L5:
Cambridge and Watertown are important centers of Armenian culture in the Greater Boston area. While Cambridge is widely known for its universities, diverse neighborhoods, and international community, nearby Watertown has long been home to one of the most established Armenian-American communities in the United States.

Armenian churches, cultural organizations, restaurants, bakeries, and community centers help preserve the language, traditions, and history of the Armenian people. Institutions such as the Armenian Museum of America in Watertown offer visitors an opportunity to explore Armenian art and heritage. Together, Cambridge and Watertown provide a welcoming environment where Armenian culture remains vibrant while continuing to evolve within contemporary American life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person prose poem about a Black woman’s lonely, disorienting first week in Cambridge, blending racism, hunger, immigrant markets, migraines, music, and vivid surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
On my first morning in Cambridge, the sky hangs low as an unwashed sheet, and every brick building looks like it has memorized a language I was not taught. I walk beneath elms that toss their shadows across me like nets. Bicycles hiss past. The bells pronounce the hour with old, white mouths.

In the café, a woman looks through me to ask who is next. I am next. I have been next for centuries. Still, the line moves around my body as if I am a stone in a river, something dark and inconvenient the water has learned to divide itself around.

By noon, hunger becomes a second skeleton. It clacks inside me. My money is thin; my pride, thinner. I follow the smell of cumin and hot oil toward the immigrant markets, where mangoes glow in their crates like captive suns and plantains lie curved as sleeping green moons. There are sacks of rice big enough to bury a child’s homesickness. A man behind the counter speaks three languages into the phone and smiles at me in a fourth. For a moment, I am not foreign. For a moment, the world is only cilantro, red pepper, fish on ice, the soft thunder of hands weighing what can be afforded.

Then the migraine arrives.

It opens behind my left eye like a black umbrella. The fluorescent lights grow teeth. The aisles tilt; tins of tomatoes float upward in small red planets. My mother’s voice comes through the ceiling, telling me to eat, baby, eat something, but the ceiling is the Charles River now, and rowers pass overhead with their white oars dipping into the air. I press my fingers to my temple as if I can hold my skull together by tenderness alone.

At night, my room is so quiet I can hear the radiator dreaming of Africa. I play Coltrane low, then Nina, then a bass line that walks barefoot through the floorboards. Music makes a door where the wall has refused me. I step through. On the other side, my grandmothers are dancing in a kitchen made of stars. Their aprons are constellations. Their laughter shakes flour onto the moon.

But morning returns with its polished shoes.

A professor touches my hair without asking. A man on the street asks where I am really from. A cashier watches my hands instead of my face. Everywhere, I am made both spectacle and shadow: too visible to rest, too invisible to be held. Cambridge rearranges itself around me—college gates becoming ribs, libraries becoming locked jaws, the river a long mirror that will not keep my reflection.

I walk anyway.

I eat a bruised pear on a bench while rain stitches silver wounds into the pavement. I count my coins. I count the Black faces passing: one, then none, then one again, each a lighthouse flickering across cold water. I want to stop them, to ask, How did you teach your loneliness to breathe here? Instead, we nod—the smallest hymn, the quickest shelter.

By the seventh day, I have learned that hunger has many dialects. The stomach’s hollow drum. The ache to be recognized. The craving for a room where my name does not arrive before me carrying its own defense. I have learned that a migraine can turn the sun into a siren, that racism can be quiet as snow, that exile sometimes smells like ripe papaya split open under market light.

I have not learned Cambridge.

But I have begun to leave crumbs of myself along its streets: a hum beneath an archway, a strand of hair on a blue scarf, my laughter startling pigeons into flight. At dusk, they rise around me—hundreds of gray wings, beating the air into pages.

For one impossible second, the whole city opens like a book.

And there I am, black ink, still wet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the experience of racial isolation in Cambridge through fragmented autobiographical memories, ending with the image of “red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.”
counterfactuals.output:
At the college gate, the porter looked past me for the student whose bag I must have been carrying.

A supervision room: portraits browned by varnish, old men watching from gilt frames. I became careful with my vowels. I learned that silence could be mistaken for ignorance and speech for anger.

In winter, the Cam held the colour of cutlery. Bicycles hissed over wet streets. I counted other brown faces without meaning to—one in the library, two outside the market, another reflected beside mine in a shop window. We never spoke. Recognition felt too intimate.

Someone asked where I was really from. Someone praised my English. At dinner, a joke crossed the table and everybody laughed; I understood it only when they turned to see whether I had laughed too.

I remember my mother’s voice on the telephone, travelling through static, making a small warm country inside the cold room. I remember spices hidden in a drawer because the corridor complained about smells. I remember dressing for May Week and feeling like a footnote in borrowed black.

Yet there were evenings when a trumpet opened above the traffic, fierce and homesick, and for a moment the city’s stone certainty cracked. I walked toward the music, toward red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary monologue in which a newly arrived woman searches for food, community, and belonging while navigating hostility and solitude in the Boston area.
counterfactuals.output:
The first thing I learned about Boston was that the wind knows when you are new.

It found the opening between my scarf and my coat as I came out of South Station, carrying one suitcase and the address of a cousin who had already moved away. The wind slipped its cold finger down my neck and said, You do not belong here. Not yet.

I had eaten nothing since morning but two crackers saved from the airplane. In the station, the restaurants shone above me in English: bowls photographed larger than faces, sandwiches stacked like houses. I counted the bills in my wallet. The numbers were familiar, but their value was not. Hunger makes an accountant of you. It makes every smell an accusation.

Outside, people walked quickly, as if late for lives that had begun without me. I asked a man where I could find a cheap market. He looked at my mouth while I spoke, not my eyes.

“What?”

I repeated myself.

He pointed somewhere behind him without stopping. Perhaps that was his kindness. Perhaps the city teaches kindness to keep moving.

For three days I lived in a room in Dorchester with walls the color of old teeth. The radiator struck its pipes at night, furious about something. I answered it in my own language.

“Yes,” I told it. “I also object.”

There was a hot plate by the window and one bent pot under the sink. I went searching for rice, onions, the red spice my mother rubbed between her fingers before dropping it into oil. In one grocery store, the shelves held twenty kinds of cereal and no food I recognized as comfort. In another, the cashier followed me down the aisle, pretending to arrange cans wherever I stood.

I wanted to turn and say: I am hungry, not criminal. I am lonely, not dangerous. I have crossed an ocean carrying photographs, certificates no one here will honor, and my mother’s last message folded in my mind. Do you think I came all this way for your canned beans?

But I said nothing. Silence was the first local currency I learned to spend.

Then, one evening, I smelled garlic frying.

It came through the cold near Fields Corner, warm and insistent, from a narrow shop with fogged windows. Inside were sacks of rice, green herbs tied with rubber bands, fish packed in ice, jars whose labels offered alphabets I could not read. Yet I understood everything. A market is a country with many borders and one common law: someone must eat.

The woman behind the counter asked me where I was from.

I hesitated. That question can be a door or a knife.

When I told her, she nodded as if I had named a town just across the river. She called to a man stacking oranges. He called to someone in the back. Soon they were debating which bus would take me to a store in Cambridge that sold the spice I wanted. They disagreed loudly and with affection. One drew a map on the back of a receipt. Another gave me three chilies for free.

“Too hot,” the woman warned.

“No,” I said. “Not hot enough.”

She laughed, and for the first time since arriving, I heard my own laughter come back to me from another person.

Still, belonging did not happen like sunrise. It came badly, by inches.

A landlord told me my cooking smelled “strong.” A woman on the train moved her bag when I sat beside her, though the carriage was crowded. Boys shouted something from a passing car—words I understood only after I looked them up, which was worse. At work, people shortened my name without asking. They praised my English as if I had performed a trick.

Some nights I walked along the harbor because water is the only thing that can make two distant places feel adjacent. The ocean there was black, shouldering against the city. Across it was everything I had left: my mother’s courtyard, the market where vendors shouted over mountains of tomatoes, my sisters eating from one plate, the afternoon heat resting on the roofs.

Behind me, Boston glittered with windows I could not enter.

I stood between the two and belonged to neither.

But then winter loosened.

At the library, I met a woman who invited me to a church basement in Roxbury, though she did not ask if I believed in God. “We cook on Thursdays,” she said. “That’s all the faith required.”

There were twelve of us the first night. Twelve women, twelve accents, twelve versions of rice. We chopped onions and told partial stories. No one demanded the whole truth. One woman had left a husband. One had buried a son. One sent half her wages home. One had been in Boston twenty-seven years and still called another place home.

I cooked my mother’s stew in a pot large enough to bathe a child.

When I opened the spice, the room changed. Not into my old kitchen—nothing can restore what distance has taken—but into a new place, made from fragments. A borrowed knife. A dented table. Snow melting from our boots. Someone humming off-key. Someone else asking for the recipe.

We ate from mismatched bowls.

“This tastes like somewhere,” a woman said.

I nearly cried.

Now, when newcomers ask me where to buy food, I do not point while walking away. I take them if I can. I show them the cheap market, the good fish, the bus that is always late. I warn them about the wind. I tell them which streets feel unfriendly after dark and which doors will open if they knock.

I have learned that a city does not welcome you once. It welcomes you in pieces, and sometimes you must welcome yourself.

So I keep onions in the cupboard. Rice in a blue tin. Chilies drying above the sink. On Thursdays, I make too much food.

I am still lonely sometimes. I still hear my name mispronounced. There are days when every brick in Boston seems to say, Not yours.

But I have a key now.

I have a bowl with my name written underneath it.

I have people who notice when I am absent.

And when the wind finds the space between my scarf and coat, I pull the cloth tighter and keep walking.

Let it test me.

I know where I am going.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental memoir passage about being a person of color in an overwhelmingly white city, using sensory details from Armenian markets, Chinese restaurants, Wagner, samba, and public transportation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Transfer Point**

The city called itself clean. By this it meant pale stone, pale faces, winter packed into the seams of the sidewalks. Even the pigeons looked powdered.

On the tram, I became punctuation.

A dark mark between two blond sentences.

**Next stop: Hauptbahnhof. Please exit on the right.**

At the Armenian market, apricots glowed like small captured suns. I pressed one with my thumb and smelled the split skin: honey, dust, the faint sourness of travel. Behind the counter, jars of sour cherries stood shoulder to shoulder with pickled peppers and grape leaves folded into tight green parcels. The shopkeeper spoke to me in Armenian. I answered in the city’s language. For a second we were both embarrassed, though neither of us had done anything wrong.

Outside, snow erased the curb.

Inside, the coffee was black and granular. It left a little earth at the bottom of the cup.

*

People asked where I was from, then where I was *really* from, as if my first answer were a train station and not a destination. Their curiosity arrived smiling. It removed its gloves.

I learned to say: Here.

I learned to say it without apology.

*

In the Chinese restaurant near the opera house, steam clouded the windows until the white city disappeared. Chili oil shone red beneath fluorescent light. Star anise, vinegar, garlic, scorched scallions—the air struck the back of my throat and opened something there. Plates collided in the kitchen. A cleaver kept time.

At the next table, two women discussed Wagner, his storms and gods, his magnificent machinery of doom. Later, in the opera house, the brass rose like a wall of fire. The music demanded surrender. Around me, velvet sleeves, silver hair, perfume with the dry sweetness of dead flowers.

I watched the Valkyries ride.

I watched the audience believe it had invented thunder.

During intermission, a man asked if I understood the opera.

I said, “Enough.”

What I meant was: I understand siege. I understand longing dressed as destiny. I understand what it is to enter a room already carrying someone else’s idea of you.

The bell rang. We returned to our assigned seats.

*

**Please keep your belongings with you at all times.**

My belongings:

one name repeatedly mispronounced  
three languages, none considered sufficient  
the apricot’s bruised gold  
the restaurant window breathing white  
a tram pass creased at the month  
my mother’s warning not to make trouble  
my father’s warning not to disappear

*

In summer, samba spilled from a basement bar beneath the railway tracks. The drummer’s palms struck the skin; the room answered with hips, heels, sweat. For once, nobody moved as if watched. Or everyone moved because we were watched and had decided to survive the gaze by becoming radiant.

The floor smelled of beer and rain-damp coats. A woman in a yellow dress pulled me into the circle. The rhythm entered through my soles, climbed my shins, loosened the careful architecture of my body.

Above us, trains passed, shaking dust from the ceiling.

Below, we made another city.

Not whiter. Not cleaner.

Alive.

*

On the night bus home, I saw my face in the glass laid over the city’s reflection: my eyes floating among lit apartments, closed bakeries, statues green with weather. Each streetlamp passed through my forehead. Each darkened shop occupied my chest.

Across the aisle, a child stared at me. Her mother whispered something. The child kept staring.

I smiled.

She smiled back.

It was not redemption. It was not a bridge. It was simply two faces briefly unafraid of each other while the bus sighed at a red light.

Then the doors opened.

Cold rushed in, metallic and bright. Someone boarded carrying a bag of oranges. Someone got off humming a melody I recognized but could not name.

**Final stop. All passengers must leave the vehicle.**

The city insisted I was passing through.

I stepped down anyway, into the snow, carrying its music in my mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic stream-of-consciousness scene beginning with a racist road incident in Cambridge and moving through loneliness, fainting from hunger, encounters with immigrants, and fantasies of rescue.
counterfactuals.output:
The van slows beside me on Mill Road, window cranking down like the lid of a bad eye, and the man leans out to throw a country at my face as if it were rubbish, as if my skin were an address he could mispronounce and hate. His friends laugh. The light changes. They surge away beneath the Cambridge rain, leaving diesel, laughter, and one crushed paper cup turning in the gutter like a small white planet with nowhere to go.

I keep walking.

Past bicycles chained in shivering rows, past colleges hoarding their yellow windows, past the river carrying its dark grammar under bridges. Everyone seems expected somewhere. Everyone has a key warm in a pocket, a soup waiting, a name spoken tenderly through a door.

My phone is dead, or I am. I cannot remember which.

Hunger begins as an animal scratching politely inside me, then loses its manners. By Parker’s Piece the lamps lengthen, kneel, rise. The pavement tilts its gray cheek toward mine. I think: so this is how the earth embraces you when no one else will.

Then nothing—

then cumin, wet wool, someone saying, Easy, sister, easy.

A woman from Aleppo lifts my head onto her folded coat. A Polish delivery rider presses orange juice into my hand. A Ghanaian nurse, late for the night shift, counts my pulse beneath the rain and scolds me with such practiced tenderness that I nearly cry. Around us, accents gather like candles protected by cupped hands.

Eat, they say.

Drink.

Stay with us.

And because I am weak, I obey. Because I am lonely, I pretend these strangers have been looking for me all evening, crossing borders, surviving boats, airports, interviews, rooms with hostile clocks—only to arrive here, at this exact patch of cold grass, where I have fallen out of the world.

The juice is too sweet. It burns like sunrise.

An ambulance is coming, someone says, and immediately I imagine more than an ambulance: a white ship gliding over the rooftops, a ladder lowered from the moon, my mother stepping down in the dress she wore before worry bent her shoulders. I imagine the river reversing, every slammed door opening, the van returning so the men can climb out ashamed, carrying bread.

I imagine Cambridge unbuilding its walls stone by stone.

But there is only the siren, nearer now, blue light washing the ancient buildings clean for half a second at a time. The woman from Aleppo holds my hand. Her palm is warm and real.

No angel arrives.

No prince.

Only people the city has taught to be invisible, making a small country around my body, refusing to let me disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
